description_full: COPT Defense Properties is a self-managed REIT focused on owning, operating and developing properties in locations proximate to, or sometimes containing, key U.S. Government defense installations and missions (referred to as its Defense/IT Portfolio). The Company's tenants include the USG and their defense contractors, who are primarily engaged in priority national security activities, and who generally require mission-critical and high security property enhancements. As of September 30, 2026, the Company's Defense/IT Portfolio of 202 properties, including 24 owned through unconsolidated joint ventures, encompassed 23.3 million square feet and was 96.2% leased. COPT Defense Properties was incorporated in 1988 and is based in Columbia, United States.

Each employee generates $672K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $27K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: COPT Defense Properties is a mid-cap real estate business with a $3.8B market cap on $764M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $289M in free cash flow — roughly 38 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 32% operating margin runs 9pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 21% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.53, it is more defensive than the market.

val: The stock trades 38% below its DCF fair value of $53.09, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 56%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $37.88 to $75.95 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/FCF 13.3 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 11% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $39.12 on average, 18% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
It converts 38% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.04x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 38%.
ROE of 10% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 8pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 6.1x net debt to EBITDA ($275.0M of cash against $2.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.07 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.1% over 3 years, 4.6% over 5 years and 2.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.10 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 22% of annual revenue and FFO growth of 5.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 41, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (3.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 34 consecutive years, raising it 2.1% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 12.8% of the float, 12.6 days to cover.
people: With about 430 employees, each generates about $1.8M of revenue, 0.8x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 2.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $672K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
